hook.text: If you fell into a small black hole, tidal forces would stretch you into a thin strand—like spaghetti.

buildup.text: Gravity pulls harder on your feet than your head. The difference grows as you approach, stretching you vertically.

discovery.text: Stephen Hawking coined the term 'spaghettification.' It's a real physics concept with an unforgettable name.

twist.text: Supermassive black holes are gentler. Their tidal forces at the horizon are weak—you'd cross without being stretched.

climax.text: But you still couldn't escape. You'd fall toward the singularity and be crushed in a fraction of a second.

punchline.text: Small black holes stretch you. Big ones swallow you whole.

quiz.question: Why is spaghettification less severe at a supermassive black hole?
options: The tidal forces at the event horizon are weaker because the black hole is much larger
Supermassive black holes don't have event horizons
The rotation of supermassive black holes cancels out tidal forces

details.summary: Spaghettification is the extreme stretching of objects falling into a black hole, caused by tidal forces — gravity pulling stronger on the closer side than the far side. Near a stellar-mass black hole, a human would be stretched into a thin strand of atoms long before reaching the event horizon.
details.whyItMatters: Spaghettification vividly demonstrates how extreme tidal forces become near compact objects, making abstract gravitational physics tangible and illustrating why black holes are the universe's most violent environments.
takeaways: Tidal forces stretch objects into thin strands near black holes
Gravity pulls harder on the near side than the far side
Smaller black holes produce stronger tidal forces at the horizon

faq.question: Would you feel spaghettification falling into a supermassive black hole?
faq.answer: Surprisingly, no — at least not at the event horizon. Because supermassive black holes are so large, tidal forces at the horizon are gentle. You could cross the event horizon of a billion-solar-mass black hole without noticing. Spaghettification would occur much later, closer to the singularity.

faq.question: Has spaghettification ever been observed?
faq.answer: Yes, indirectly. In 2020, astronomers observed a tidal disruption event where a star was torn apart by a supermassive black hole. The star was stretched and compressed into a thin stream of gas that spiraled into the black hole, producing a months-long flare of light.
